column4: The earth itself is أَرْضَ خَاشِعَةً, then water makes it stir and swell; the verse states outright the section's transfer between a humbled dry face, watered soil, and resurrection.
The reader sees lifeless earth, rain, stirring, swelling, and lovely growth; this is the full dry-to-soft soil process heard behind the two faces.
Good land yields growth by its Lord's leave while bad land yields only scantily; the one rain discloses two soils just as the Day discloses two kinds of face.
Hearts are asked to become تَخْشَعَ and are warned against hardening; the inner softness behind bodily khushu is set beside the revived earth in 57:17.
Allah gives the earth life after its death; following 57:16, the soil's softening interprets how a hardened heart can become humble.
The doers of excellence have faces covered by neither dust nor abasement, the exact negative boundary of the dust-soiled, lowered face developed in the section.
The evildoers' faces are covered by abasement and seem cut from dark night, completing 10:26's face division with the darkened counterpart.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاضِرَةٌ gives the same Day-of-Judgment subject and makes freshness visible directly on the face.
وَوُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَاسِرَةٌ places the scowling face opposite the fresh face of 75:22, matching the section's paired openings.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ joins a face and settled dust explicitly, making the commentary's dusty-land hearing visible.
نَضْرَةَ النَّعِيمِ is recognizable on the blessed faces; the نعيم family itself supplies the freshness carried by ناعمة.
Allah meets the patient with نَضْرَةً وَسُرُورًا, joining fresh appearance to the joy from which the section hears the couch's name and reversing marked grief.
They fall upon their faces weeping and revelation increases them in خُشُوعًا; face, bodily lowering, and inward humility occur in one act.
وَعَنَتِ الْوُجُوهُ depicts all faces bowed before the Living, Self-Sustaining on the Day, a nonlexical parallel to the lowered face.
The condemned are خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ and look furtively when exposed to the Fire; khushu here is visibly the abasement heard in the face.
خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ describes humbled eyes as people emerge from graves, locating the same lowering in the resurrection face.
خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ and covering abasement join lowered eyes to the humiliation that the section's dry face bears.
خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ and enveloping abasement describe the promised Day, repeating the humbled-eye face scene.
أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ places khushu in the eyes of hearts terrified by resurrection, another bodily location of the lowered face.
On the Day some faces whiten and other faces blacken; the verse uses the same face-by-face division to expose opposite outcomes.
The whitened faces remain in Allah's mercy, supplying the lasting condition behind the bright half of 3:106's divided scene.
Faces that Day are bright; this is the luminous half of the face pair whose dusty half appears in 80:40.
Those bright faces are laughing and rejoicing, giving the inward joy corresponding to the section's soft, happy face.
Darkness overspreads the dust-covered faces of 80:40, showing that the dust is a condition of the whole face rather than a stray detail.
The dusty, darkened faces belong to the faithless and shameless; the verse identifies the moral outcome embodied in 80:40-41.
Hell's water is like molten metal and يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ, directly joining a face to drink that burns instead of reviving it.
The condemned circulate between Hell and حَمِيمٍ آنٍ; آنٍ is the masculine form of the source section's boiling-water adjective آنيَة.
Paradise has water whose quality does not spoil, while the condemned drink boiling water that cuts their bowels; one verse sets life-giving and destructive drink across a boundary.
In Hell they taste neither coolness nor drink, denying precisely what parched soil or a weary body needs before 78:25 names the substitute.
إِلَّا حَمِيمًا وَغَسَّاقًا replaces cool drink with boiling water and foul fluid, closely matching the section's reversed watering.
وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ repeats the exclusive 'no food except' construction of the ضريع verse with another punitive food.
Only sinners eat the غسلين of 69:36; the verse fixes the eater and punitive function of that exclusive food.
A defiant person has Hell ahead and is given purulent water to drink, another watering that torments rather than restores.
Boiling water is poured from above their heads, making destructive water descend where rain should enliven what lies below.
Job names his affliction نُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ, using the section's fatigue root for bodily suffering before 38:42 answers it with cool water.
A cool washing place and drink relieve Job's نُصْب in 38:41; this water heals the exhausted body, the direct reverse of the boiling spring.
The people of the garden sit عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُتَقَابِلِينَ after rancor is removed, joining the named couch to reconciled repose before fatigue is excluded.
لَا يَمَسُّهُمْ فِيهَا نَصَبٌ denies fatigue in that garden, reversing the exhausted laboring condition.
The garden people praise Allah for removing الْحَزَنَ, the grief that the section says can leave its trace as fatigue before 35:35 excludes fatigue itself.
لَا يَمَسُّنَا فِيهَا نَصَبٌ وَلَا ... لُغُوبٌ removes both fatigue and weariness from the lasting home.
كَانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُورًا tells the blessed that their striving is appreciated, stating why a face can be satisfied with its effort.
Whoever seeks the Hereafter and strives its proper striving in faith has a striving that is appreciated, the positive counterpart to exhausted labor.
A human being has only what he strives for; this makes the final face's relation to its own سعي accountable rather than decorative.
A person's striving will be seen, the disclosure that connects present labor to the face that bears its result.
The striving will receive the fullest recompense, completing the sequence that makes satisfaction with one's effort intelligible.
Humanity is laboring painfully toward its Lord and will meet Him; this gathers work, weariness, return, and encounter into one line.
Receiving the record in the right hand begins the favorable outcome of the labor named in 84:6.
An easy accounting explains how the laborer's meeting in 84:6 leads toward joy rather than exhausted abasement.
The one easily accounted returns مَسْرُورًا, the same joy root used to explain the couch's name and the end of grief.
Some people's striving is lost in the nearer life while they think they act well; it explains how work can culminate in exhaustion rather than satisfaction.
فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ uses the same رضو root for a pleasing life after the record is received, extending satisfaction from effort to its abode.
فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ again makes the final life itself pleasing after the weighing of deeds.
The soul returns رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً, both satisfied and approved, clarifying the two directions that رضى can take at the return.
After giving to be purified and seeking his Lord's face, the servant وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ; future satisfaction is tied to prior action.
Neighboring plots and gardens are watered with one water yet differ in produce; water reveals differing earth just as the Day reveals differing faces.
Water descends, travels as springs in the earth, raises crops, and then the crops yellow and crumble; the verse gives the entire wet-soft-to-dry cycle.
Winds carry heavy cloud to dead land, rain descends, and fruits emerge; sky, moist wind, water, and reviving soil meet in one scene.
Winds raise cloud, Allah drives it to dead country and revives the earth; the verse also names this as the likeness of resurrection.
Rain revives earth after death, winds are turned, and cloud is held between sky and earth, assembling the section's full sky-water-soil relation.
Earlier peoples were seized with hardship and adversity so that they might humble themselves, using the ض ر ع family to connect suffering with abasement.
They failed to humble themselves when hardship came because their hearts hardened; hard-hearted refusal marks the boundary before compelled abasement.
Towns are seized with hardship and adversity so that their people might humble themselves, repeating the punitive setting of the ضريع root's abasement sense.
Even when punishment grips them, they neither submit nor تَضَرَّعُونَ; refusal of voluntary abasement contrasts with the lowered faces of judgment.
Thirst, fatigue, and hunger endured in God's path are recorded as righteous work; unlike futile exhausted labor, this نَصَب has a preserved outcome.
Moses' attendant says the journey has brought them نَصَبًا, preserving the root's plain bodily sense of fatigue from prolonged exertion.
Voices become خَشَعَتْ before the Merciful on the Day; the root shifts from face or earth to sound while keeping the sense of lowered stillness.
A mountain would become خَاشِعًا and split from fear of Allah; even a hard raised body can be lowered and broken open.
Skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance after shivering, supplying an inward softening opposite the hardened heart and dry-earth condition.
Hardened hearts are likened to stones, yet some stones gush rivers, split to release water, or fall in awe; hardness, water, opening, and lowering are held together.
Prayer and patience are difficult except for الْخَاشِعِينَ, locating khushu in the receptive person whose inward state governs the body.
Rain mingles with earth's growth until the adorned land is suddenly reaped bare, a compressed wet flourishing and drying image for the passing life.
Fertilizing winds are sent and water descends from the sky for people to drink; it supplies the humid-wind and sky-as-water side of the image.
Water from the sky gives earth life after death, one of the Quran's repeated direct formulations of the section's soil transformation.
Worldly life is rain, mingled vegetation, then dry fragments scattered by wind; softness and greenness are explicitly temporary.
Rain descends and the earth becomes green, a concise visual change from dryness to living softness.
Winds announce mercy and pure water descends from the sky, preparing the dead-land revival stated in 25:49.
The pure water gives life to dead country and drink to creatures, uniting revived soil with the ordinary life-giving purpose of watering.
Water from the sky revives earth after death; the repeated sign anchors the face-soil image in a general divine pattern.
Allah brings living from dead and revives earth after its death, placing the soil process beside human emergence.
Lightning brings fear and hope, then rain revives dead earth; the water's arrival stands between dread and mercy.
Winds raise and spread cloud, rain comes through it, and people rejoice when it reaches whom Allah wills; moist wind leads to joy as well as softened land.
The addressee is told to look at the effects of mercy in earth revived after death, making observation of transformed ground evidence for resurrection.
Water is driven to barren land and crops emerge for livestock and people; provision appears from ground previously unable to grow.
Dead earth is given life and produces grain that people eat, joining resurrection, soil, and nourishing food.
Gardens are made in the revived earth and springs are caused to burst within them, adding the flowing-eye result to 36:33.
Measured water descends from the sky and revives dead country, followed by the promise that people will likewise be brought out.
Provision descends from the sky and revives earth after death, with the turning winds named beside it as a sign.
Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and harvested grain, beginning a provision scene that ends in resurrection.
Tall date palms with layered clusters show the fresh abundance produced by the blessed water of 50:9.
The growth is provision, dead land is revived by water, and human emergence is likened to it; the sequence completes the image's implication.
Rain-fed growth delights its cultivators, then dries, yellows, and becomes debris; the soft fresh condition is set within its earthly limit.
Abundant water is poured from rain clouds, beginning a compact sky-to-earth sequence.
The poured water brings forth grain and vegetation, showing its nourishing rather than burning effect.
Dense gardens are the mature result of the water and growth in 78:14-15.
The earth is spread after the sky is built, matching the section's paired invitation to look at sky and laid-out ground.
Water and pasture are brought out from that earth, showing what the spread ground holds when made life-bearing.
Water is poured abundantly, opening another Quranic soil sequence just before the same surah's two kinds of face.
The earth is split open, the receptive action by which the water of 80:25 becomes growth.
Grain is caused to grow in the opened, watered earth, distinguishing nourishing water from the punitive drink.
Allah brings out pasture, the fresh phase of the earth image before its reversal in 87:5.
The pasture becomes dark stubble, reversing softness and freshness into the dried residue of earthly growth.
Water descends by measure and is lodged in the earth, while Allah can take it away; flowing moisture is a held provision rather than an entitlement.
If water sinks away, no one can bring flowing water; it marks the boundary between a land with an accessible spring and one deprived of it.
A flourishing garden may become bare, slippery ground, showing fertile softness stripped away under judgment.
Its water may sink so deep that it cannot be recovered, completing 18:40's reversal from garden to unusable ground.
The God-conscious are in gardens and springs; this is the setting whose couches and freedom from fatigue appear in 15:47-48.
The God-conscious dwell securely among gardens and springs, repeating the garden-plus-water-eye scene.
The God-conscious are amid gardens and springs, another concise placement of the blessed in watered ground.
The two gardens contain two flowing springs, closely matching the section's عَيْنٌ جَارِيَةٌ.
Two other gardens contain two gushing springs, preserving the water-eye while distinguishing its mode of flow.
The righteous drink from a spring whose flow they cause to gush abundantly; the spring is both drink and freely running source.
A spring in the garden is named Salsabil, continuing the blessed drink sequence as the counterpart of the boiling spring.
The God-conscious are amid shades and springs, joining shelter and available water in the final abode.
A cup from a flowing source is passed around the garden company, contrasting communal pleasant drink with forced burning drink.
Cups, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing source are carried among the blessed near the couches of 56:15-16.
The sincere servants sit on couches facing one another, preserving the couch as a social scene of untroubled joy.
Couches appear among the silver furnishings that could have been universal worldly luxury, testing the assumption that the object itself guarantees blessedness.
Those furnishings are only enjoyment of the nearer life, while the Hereafter with the Lord is for the God-conscious; it supplies the couch's moral boundary.
The blessed recline on arranged couches, another fulfillment of the resting object whose name the section relates to joy.
The foremost are on woven couches, placing the object at the center of their repose.
They recline on those couches facing one another, completing the restful communal scene begun in 56:15.
The righteous are in نعيم, the condition whose freshness becomes readable on their faces in 83:24.
They look out from couches, linking restful seating to the face whose radiance is identified in the following verse.
The rewarded recline on couches and experience neither sun nor bitter cold, giving the seat a temperate, restful environment.
The Quran asks whether garden hospitality or the tree of Zaqqum is better, setting blessed provision against punitive food before 37:66-67.
The condemned eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies, another food whose function is punishment rather than nourishment.
Their food is followed by a mixture of boiling water, pairing punitive eating and drinking as in the section.
The condemned are told to taste boiling water and foul fluid, repeating the destructive drink pair.
They are dragged in boiling water and then burned in the Fire, making hot water part of the punishment itself.
The tree of Zaqqum is introduced as the food at the start of a food-and-boiling-water punishment sequence.
Zaqqum is called the food of the sinful, directly identifying the eater and punitive meal.
The food is like molten metal in bellies, turning ingestion into internal burning rather than nourishment.
It boils like the boiling of scalding water, joining the punitive food's effect to the section's heated spring.
Boiling-water punishment is poured over the sinner's head, completing the sequence begun with Zaqqum.
The straying deniers eat from the tree of Zaqqum, beginning another explicit food-and-hot-water pair.
They fill their bellies from that tree, emphasizing a meal that gives no wholesome nourishment.
They then drink boiling water upon the food, the same punitive conjunction of eating and watering.
They drink like desperately thirsty camels, showing that the hot drink does not resolve the thirst that drives them to it.
Those taken by their religion as play have a drink of boiling water for their disbelief, another direct occurrence of punitive drink.
Those who disbelieve have boiling drink and painful punishment, set after the promise of just recompense for belief and good work.
The boiling water melts what is in their bellies and their skins, spelling out the bodily effect of the pouring in 22:19.
The condemned person tries to sip the purulent water but can scarcely swallow it, showing the impossibility of relief in that drink.
Following Allah's رضوان is contrasted with returning under divine wrath, enacting the dictionary opposition named for ر ض و.
They follow what angers Allah and dislike His رضوان, so their deeds are nullified; approval and wrath govern whether labor endures.
On the Day of truth, eternal gardens accompany Allah being pleased with the truthful and their being pleased with Him, making satisfaction reciprocal.
After gardens and lasting dwellings, رضوان from Allah is called greater; the pleasing abode does not exhaust the meaning of satisfaction.
Eternal gardens culminate in Allah being pleased with the faithful and their being pleased with Him, another final mutual satisfaction.
The Lord promises to give until the addressee is satisfied, presenting رضى as the response to a future divine gift rather than to one's own labor.
The deafening blast announces the moment at which the opposed faces of 80:38-42 appear; its own contribution is the event that changes the scene.
